name: Maitra's Rotating Dust
description: A stationary, cylindrically symmetric universe of dust that turns faster near its axis than far from it, found by Samaresh C. Maitra in 1966. It has no cosmological constant and no closed timelike curves, and its density falls from $c^2/8\pi Ga^2$ on the axis toward zero far away.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Maitra's universe is dust and nothing else, turning steadily about one axis, fast near the axis and more slowly far from it [maitra1966, chan2024]. Nothing in it expands or collapses, and the dust needs neither pressure nor a cosmological constant to hold its place: every grain circles the axis in free fall [chan2024]. Its author, Samaresh C. Maitra, was at the University of Maryland, where he took his doctorate under Charles Misner in 1968 [maitra1966, mathgenealogymaitra]. He put the selling point in the title of his paper of 1966, a cosmological solution "with $\Lambda = 0$ and without Closed Timelike Lines" [maitra1966].¶Why advertise the lack of something? Two earlier universes of rotating dust both let a traveler meet her own past [vanstockum1937, godel1949]. In Willem Jacob van Stockum's cylinder of 1937 a rocket far enough from the axis can circle around to the event it left [vanstockum1937]. Kurt Gödel's universe of 1949 allows the same trip through every one of its events, and it needs a negative cosmological constant besides [godel1949]. Maitra's universe has no cosmological constant, and no closed timelike curve passes through any of its events [maitra1966].¶How does his dust get away with it? Van Stockum's dust and Gödel's turn rigidly, like a wheel, and far from the axis their light cones tip over until a circle around the axis lies inside them [vanstockum1937, godel1949]. Maitra's dust shears: it turns as water does around a drain, each ring at its own rate, sliding past the rings on either side [chan2024]. Its light cones lean the way the dust goes, more and more with distance, and at no distance do they lean far enough to take in a circle, so no path a traveler could follow returns to its start [maitra1966, chan2024]. Shear is paid for in matter, since it lowers the density that a given rotation can support, and Maitra's dust is densest on the axis and thins out with distance [chan2024].¶"Analytic and complete" was Maitra's own description of his solution, and by 1968 a third word had joined those two: his thesis is titled "A Stationary and Complete, but Unstable, Inhomogeneous Cosmological Solution of Einstein's Equations" [maitra1966, mathgenealogymaitra]. Other dust of the same symmetry behaves worse [king1974, vishveshwara1977]. With one function left free to choose, the general stationary solution for dust with cylindrical symmetry came in 1974 from A. R. King at University College London, who spent the freedom on "new types of singularity" [king1974]. The next year Jeffrey Winicour reduced every stationary rotating dust with an axis of symmetry to quadratures [winicour1975]. He and C. V. Vishveshwara followed light through the fastest cylinders in 1977, where the cones sent out from the axis turn around and refocus on it, and they tied the refocusing to "acausal behavior" [vishveshwara1977].¶Andrzej Krasiński, sorting rotating dust by its symmetries in 1998, found Maitra's solution among King's, marked off by a timelike Killing field of unit length and by two further conditions, of which he wrote that he "was not able to interpret" them "in invariant terms" [krasinski1998rotating]. Could a spinning cylinder of the stuff sit in empty space? William Bonnor and B. R. Steadman tried it: they cut the universe off at a finite radius, fitted a vacuum around it, and reported "no closed timelike curves in the interior or exterior" [bonnor2009maitra, maccallum2015]. Deriving the solution afresh in 2024 by integrating the field equations directly, R. Chan and N. O. Santos showed that it is the only stationary, cylindrically symmetric dust with shear whose axis is regular [chan2024]. They also found that the vacuum around such a cylinder has to belong to the Weyl class of Thomas Lewis's solutions, and that shearing dust packs less mass into each unit of length than rigid dust can [lewis1932, chan2024].

related.text: Willem Jacob van Stockum's cylinder of dust in rigid rotation, whose circles about the axis are closed timelike curves beyond $r = R$. Maitra's dust is that cylinder allowed to shear, and near the axis its line element is van Stockum's at $R = 2a$ [vanstockum1937, chan2024].
Kurt Gödel's rotating dust of 1949, homogeneous, with a negative cosmological constant and closed timelike curves through every event. Maitra's dust has neither [godel1949, maitra1966].

Charged dust in rigid rotation with no cosmological constant, where the circles about any grain are closed timelike curves beyond $r = c/\Omega$. Maitra's dust carries no charge and shears, and its circles stay spacelike [som1968, chan2024].

William Bonnor's cloud of rigidly rotating dust, flat far away, with a singular centre and closed timelike curves around it. Bonnor and B. R. Steadman later fitted a vacuum around a cylinder of Maitra's dust and found no closed timelike curves inside or out [bonnor1977cloud, bonnor2009maitra].
The vacuum around a cylinder of Maitra's dust cut off at a finite radius. R. Chan and N. O. Santos showed that it has to be of the Weyl class of Lewis's solutions [lewis1932, chan2024].
The dust thinned to nothing, $a \to \infty$, where $k$ and $\gamma$ vanish and the line element is flat space in cylindrical coordinates [chan2024].

coordinates.name: Cylindrical

parameters.description: The one length of the solution: the density of the dust on the axis is $\rho_0 = c^2/8\pi G a^2$
A function of the radius that is $1$ on the axis and grows as $2r/a$ far from it; the density of the dust is $c^2/8\pi G$ times the Ricci scalar, $\rho = 4\rho_0\,e^{-\gamma}/s(s + 1)^2$
The twist of the chart, a length, with $dk/dr = 2r/a(s + 1)$, which is less than $1$; so $k < r$ at every radius, and $g^{tt} = -(1 - k^2/r^2)$ is negative everywhere
The logarithm of the factor on $dr^2 + dz^2$, with $d\gamma/dr = -2r/a^2(s + 1)^2$; it vanishes on the axis and falls as $-\tfrac{1}{2}\ln(r/a)$ far from it

coordinates.convention: We use Maitra's cylindrical coordinates $(t, r, \phi, z)$ about the axis of rotation, in the letters of Chan and Santos, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, $\phi$ periodic in $2\pi$, and $r$ chosen so that the metric of $t$ and $\phi$ alone has the determinant $-r^2$. The lines of constant $r$, $\phi$, and $z$ are geodesics along which $t$ is proper time, and the dust circles the axis through them toward $-\phi$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
